Remark 3.40
.

From the proof of Lemma
3.20
given above, we can slightly improve the statement of the lemma as follows:
For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}_{m}
, an integer
\ell-k<p\leq\ell
with
p\geq m+2
, and
\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}^{\ell}
with
p<\mathrm{supp}(\kappa)\leq\ell
, we have

\displaystyle K(\Delta^{k}(\lambda);\Delta^{k}(\lambda);\lambda+\varepsilon_{p}+\kappa)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle K(\Delta^{k}(\mu);\Delta^{k}(\mu);\mu+\kappa),

where
\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\mu}=D_{\mathfrak{r}(p)}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}.

Indeed, throughout the straightening process introduced in §
3.5.4
,
\kappa
is left unchanged because the process affects only topmost
p
rows of the diagram.

From Remark
3.40
, we obtain the following key formula:
For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}_{m}
, and a set of integers

\ell-k<p_{1}<\dots<p_{r}\leq\ell
with
p_{1}\geq m+2
, we have

(3.24)

\displaystyle K(\Delta^{k}(\lambda);\Delta^{k}(\lambda);\lambda+\varepsilon_{p_{1}}+\dots+\varepsilon_{p_{r}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle D_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{r})}\cdots D_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1})}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}.

3.5.5.
Proof of Lemma
3.17

Let
\Psi_{1},\Psi_{2}
be root ideals of
\Delta_{\ell_{1}}^{+}

and
\Delta_{\ell_{2}}^{+}
, respectively.
Let
\Psi_{1}\uplus\Psi_{2}
be the subset of
\Delta_{\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}}^{+}

defined by:

\{(i,j)\in\Delta_{\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}}^{+}\;|\;(i,j)\in\Psi_{1}\;\mbox{or}\;(i-\ell_{1},j-\ell_{1})\in\Psi_{2}\;\mbox{or}\;(i\leq\ell_{1}\;\mbox{and}\;j>\ell_{1})\}.

Let
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}_{\ell}.

Set
\Psi=\Delta^{k}(\lambda).
By the product rule
[
5
, Lemma 3.8]
, we have

(3.25)

\displaystyle g_{(1^{r})}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle K(\Psi\uplus\varnothing_{r};\Psi\uplus\varnothing_{r};\lambda+\varepsilon_{\{\ell+1,\ldots,\ell+r\}}).

By applying Diagonal Removable Lemma
[
5
, Lemma 4.13]
,
one shows that the right-hand side of (
3.25
) is identical to

(3.26)

K(\Psi^{\prime};\Psi^{\prime};\lambda+\varepsilon_{\{\ell+1,\ldots,\ell+r\}}),

where

\Psi^{\prime}=(\Delta^{k}(\lambda)\uplus\varnothing_{r})\setminus\{(i,j)\in\Delta_{\ell+r}^{+}\;|\;i\leq\ell,\;j\geq\ell,j-i\leq r-1\}
.
We can apply
[
5
, Lemma 5.3]

with

x=\ell-k+1
,
h=k-r+1

(in the notation there) to show that
(
3.26
) is identical to

(3.27)

\sum_{a=0}^{r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subset\{\ell-k+1+r-a,\ldots,\ell\}\\
|S|=a\end{subarray}}K(\Psi^{\prime\prime};L(\Psi^{\prime\prime})\sqcup S;\lambda+\varepsilon_{S}+\varepsilon_{\{\ell+1,\ldots,\ell+r-a\}}),

where

\Psi^{\prime\prime}=\Psi^{\prime}\setminus\{(i,j)\;|\;i\leq\ell,j\geq\ell,j-i\leq k\}=\Delta^{k}(\lambda)\subset\Delta^{+}_{\ell+r}

(see also the last part of the proof of
[
5
, Proposition 5.4]
).
By
Lemma
3.11
(i)
and (
3.24
),

for
S=\{p_{1}<p_{2}<\dots<p_{a}\}
,
we have

\displaystyle K(\Psi^{\prime\prime};L(\Psi^{\prime\prime})\sqcup S;\lambda+\varepsilon_{S}+\varepsilon_{\{\ell+1,\ldots,\ell+r-a\}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{S^{\prime}\subset S}(-1)^{|S\setminus S^{\prime}|}K(\Psi^{\prime\prime};L(\Psi^{\prime\prime});\lambda+\varepsilon_{S^{\prime}}+\varepsilon_{\{\ell+1,\ldots,\ell+r-a\}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{b=0}^{a}\sum_{\ell-k+1+r-a\leq p_{i_{1}}<p_{i_{2}}<\dots<p_{i_{b}}\leq\ell}(-1)^{a-b}D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a)}\cdots D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1)}D_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{i_{b}})}\cdots D_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{i_{1}})}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a)}\cdots D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1)}T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{a})}\cdots T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1})}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}.

Therefore, (
3.27
) is equal to

(3.28)

\sum_{a=0}^{r}\sum_{\ell-k+1+r-a\leq p_{1}<\cdots<p_{a}\leq\ell}D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a)}\cdots D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1)}T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{a})}\cdots T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1})}\cdot\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}.

Proposition 3.41
.

For
1\leq r\leq k
, and
\ell\in\mathbb{Z}
, we have

\sum_{a=0}^{r}\sum_{\ell-k+1+r-a\leq p_{1}<\dots<p_{a}\leq\ell}D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a)}\dots D_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1)}T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{a})}\dots T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1})}=\sum_{A\subset I,\ |A|\leq r}T_{u_{A}}.

Proof.

We first note that
for any subsequence
A_{1}
of
(\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a),\ldots,\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1))
such that

0\leq|A_{1}|\leq r-a
, and
A_{2}
of

(\mathfrak{r}(\ell),\mathfrak{r}(\ell-1),\dots,\mathfrak{r}(\ell-k+1+r-a))

such that
|A_{2}|=a
,
the concatenation
A_{1}\cdot A_{2}
is a cyclically
increasing sequence of length less than or equal to
r.

For
0\leq a\leq n\leq r
, let

X^{n}_{a}=\left\{(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\ \left|\ \begin{aligned} &\ell-k+r-a<p_{1}<\dots<p_{a}\leq\ell\\
&<p_{a+1}<\dots<p_{n}\leq\ell+r-a\end{aligned}\ \right\}\right.

Substituting
D_{p}=T_{p}+1
into the left-hand side of the equation in the proposition, we see that

\displaystyle\sum_{a=0}^{r}\sum_{\ell-k+1+r-a\leq p_{1}<\dots<p_{a}\leq\ell}(T_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+r-a)}+1)\dots(T_{\mathfrak{r}(\ell+1)}+1)T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{a})}\dots T_{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1})}

\displaystyle=\sum_{a=0}^{r}\sum_{n=a}^{r}\sum_{(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in X^{n}_{a}}T_{u_{\{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1}),\dots,\mathfrak{r}(p_{n})\}}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{r}\sum_{a=0}^{n}\sum_{(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in X^{n}_{a}}T_{u_{\{\mathfrak{r}(p_{1}),\dots,\mathfrak{r}(p_{n})\}}}.

Then it suffices to show that the map

\mathrm{rm}:\bigsqcup_{a=0}^{n}X^{n}_{a}\to\{A\subset I\,;\,|A|=n\},\quad(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\mapsto\{\overline{p_{1}},\dots,\overline{p_{n}}\},

is bijective.
For this, we identify a subset
A\subset I
with a 01-sequence
\eta_{1}\eta_{2}\cdots\eta_{k+1}\in\{0,1\}^{k+1}
by letting
\eta_{p}=0
if
\overline{p+\ell}\in A
and
\eta_{p}=1
otherwise.
Then the image of
X^{n}_{a}
by
\mathrm{rm}
is contained in the set

S^{n}_{a}:=\left\{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}\dots\eta_{k+1}\in\{0,1\}^{k+1}\,\left|\,\begin{aligned} \textstyle\sum_{p=1}^{k+1}\eta_{p}&=k+1-n,\\
\textstyle\sum_{p=1}^{r-a}\eta_{p}&=r-n\\
\eta_{r-a+1}&=1\end{aligned}\right\}\right..

For any
\eta_{1}\eta_{2}\dots\eta_{k+1}\in\bigcup_{a=0}^{n}S_{a}^{n}
, we have

a=r+1-\min\{p\,|\,\eta_{1}+\dots+\eta_{p}=r-n+1\},

which implies
S^{n}_{a}\cap S^{n}_{a^{\prime}}=\emptyset\iff a\neq a^{\prime}
.
This implies that
\mathrm{rm}
is injective as its restriction to
X^{n}_{a}
is injective.
Because
\sum_{a=0}^{n}|X^{n}_{a}|=\sum_{a=0}^{n}\binom{k-r+a}{a}\binom{r-a}{n-a}=\binom{k+1}{n}=\sharp\{A\subset I\,;\,|A|=n\}
, the map
\mathrm{rm}
is also surjective.
∎

This completes the proof of Lemma
3.17
.

4.
Relation to quantum
K
-theory

4.1.
Quantum
K
-theory ring of the flag variety

Theorem 4.1

(
[
17
]
,
[
27
]
,
[
28
]
,
[
34
]
,
[
35
]
)
.

{QK}(G/B)

can be identified with the quotient ring

(4.1)

A_{k+1}:=\mathbb{C}[[Q]][z_{1},\ldots,z_{k+1}]/I_{k+1},

where
I_{k+1}
is the ideal of
\mathbb{C}[[Q]][z_{1},\ldots,z_{k+1}]
generated by

(4.2)

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset\{1,\ldots,k+1\}\\
|I|=i\end{subarray}}\prod_{j\in I}z_{j}\!\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in I\\
j+1\notin I\end{subarray}}(1-Q_{j})-\textstyle{\binom{k+1}{i}}\quad(1\leq i\leq k+1),

such that
for
w\in S_{k+1}
the
quantum Grothendieck polynomial

\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q}
of Lenart and Maeno, with the change of variables
x_{i}=1-z_{i}
, represents
\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{w}

in
{QK}(G/B_{k+1})
.

Let
QK^{\mathrm{pol}}(G/B)
denote the

\mathbb{C}[Q]
-module spanned by
\mathcal{O}^{w}_{G/B}\;(w\in S_{k+1})
.
Let
S
be the multiplicative subset
1+(Q)
of
\mathbb{C}[Q].
For a
\mathbb{C}[Q]
-module
M
,
we denote by
M_{S}
the localization by
S.

By a result of
Anderson, Chen, Tseng, and Iritani
[
2
]
,
QK^{\mathrm{pol}}(G/B)_{S}

forms a subring of
QK(G/B)
.

Let
A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}
be the quotient ring

\mathbb{C}[Q][z_{1},\ldots,z_{k+1}]/I_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}
, where

I_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}
is the ideal of
\mathbb{C}[Q][z_{1},\ldots,z_{k+1}]
generated by
the polynomials (
4.2
).
The following result is a modified version of Kirillov-Maeno’s (conjectural) presentation
given in
[
28
, Remark in §6.1]
. For the reader’s convenience, we give a sketch of proof.

Proposition 4.2
.

There exists an isomorphism of
\mathbb{C}[Q]_{S}

algebras

(4.3)

(A^{\mathrm{pol}}_{k+1})_{S}\longrightarrow{QK}^{\mathrm{pol}}(G/B)_{S}.

Moreover the image of
\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q}
in
(A^{\mathrm{pol}}_{k+1})_{S}
is sent to
\mathcal{O}^{w}_{G/B}

for
w\in S_{k+1}.

Proof.

By
[
1
, Chapter 3, Exercise 2]
, we see that the localized ideal

(Q)_{S}
is contained in the Jacobson radical of
\mathbb{C}[Q]_{S}
.
By
[
34
, Corollary B.3(2)]
, we see that the right-hand side of (
4.3
) is finitely generated as
\mathbb{C}[Q]_{S}
-module.
Then we can apply Nakayama-type arguments (
[
11
, Proposition A.3 and Remark A.6]
) to obtain the isomorphism by the same arguments as in
[
34
, Theorem 6.1]
.
The second statement follows from

[
28
, Theorem 50]
or

[
35
, Theorem 4.4]
.
∎

4.2.
Map
\Phi_{k+1}

Recall that
\tau_{i}:=g_{R_{i}},\;\tau_{i}^{+}:=\tilde{g}_{R_{i}}
with
R_{i}=(\overbrace{i,\ldots,i}^{k+1-i})
for
1\leq i\leq k
.
Note that
the notation
R_{i}
is different from the one used in
[
13
]
, and
the indices of
\tau_{i}
are also switched from the ones in
[
13
]
by
i\mapsto k+1-i
(see Remark
4.4
below).

Theorem 4.3

(
[
13
]
)
.

There is a ring isomorphism

(4.4)

\Phi_{k+1}:A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]\longrightarrow\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1},(\tau^{+}_{i})^{-1}],

where
1\leq i\leq k,
such that

(4.5)

z_{i}\mapsto\frac{\tau_{i}\tau^{+}_{i-1}}{\tau^{+}_{i}\tau_{i-1}}\;(1\leq i\leq k+1),\quad Q_{i}\mapsto\frac{\tau_{i-1}\tau_{i+1}}{\tau_{i}^{2}}\;(1\leq i\leq k).

The map
\Phi_{k+1}
was constructed by
solving the relativistic Toda lattice equation
with the initial condition that the Lax matrix is unipotent.
Although the construction of
\Phi_{k+1}
has no apparent geometric meaning,
it is expected that
the map sends a Schubert structure sheaf
\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{w}
to
an element in
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})_{\mathrm{loc}}
related to a Schubert class.

Remark 4.4
.

Our convention for
\Phi_{k+1}
is slightly
different from the one in
[
13
]
.
Let
\overline{\Omega}
be the automorphism of
\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1},(\tau^{+}_{i})^{-1}]
given as the natural extension of
\Omega
(see §
3.1
).
One can check that
\Phi_{k+1}^{\prime}=\overline{\Omega}\circ\Phi_{k+1}
coincides with the map introduced in
[
13
]
by replacing
\sigma_{i}
in their notation with
\tau^{+}_{i}
.

Corollary 4.5
.

There is an injective
\mathbb{C}[Q]
-algebra homomorpshism

\phi:A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]\hookrightarrow QK(G/B)[Q_{i}^{-1}]

such that the image of
\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q}
in
A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]
is sent to

\mathcal{O}^{w}_{G/B}.

Proof.

We know from
Theorem
4.3
that
A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]
is an integral domain, and hence

A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]
is a
\mathbb{C}[Q]
-subalgebra of

(A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}])_{S}
, where
S=1+(Q).

Consider the composition of ring homomorphisms

\displaystyle A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow(A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}])_{S}

\displaystyle=((A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}})_{S})[Q_{i}^{-1}]

\displaystyle\cong(QK^{\mathrm{pol}}(G/B)_{S})[Q_{i}^{-1}]\quad\text{(Proposition \ref{prop:KMmodified})}

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow QK(G/B)[Q_{i}^{-1}].

The statement on
\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q}
follows from that of Proposition
4.2
.
∎

4.3.
K
-homology of the affine Grassmannian

For
x\in\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0}
, let
\xi_{x}^{0}\in K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})
be the element
defined
[
21
, §6.3]
.
The non-equivariant
K
-theoretic
k
-Schur function
g_{x}^{(k)}
in

[
21
, Theorem 7.17 (2)]
corresponds to
\xi_{x}^{0}
.
Let us denote this isomorphism by
\alpha_{\circ}:K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})\rightarrow\Lambda_{(k)}.

It holds that

\alpha_{\circ}(\mathcal{O}_{x}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{x}
(
[
39
]
,
[
20
, Lemma 2 (ii)]
).
We define a twisted isomorphism
\alpha:K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})\rightarrow\Lambda_{(k)}
by

\alpha:=\sigma^{-1}\circ\alpha_{\circ}.

Thus we have

(4.6)

\alpha(\mathcal{O}_{x}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=\sigma^{-1}(\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{x}).

Proposition 4.6
.

If
\lambda\subset R_{i}
for some
1\leq i\leq k
, equivalently

\lambda_{1}+\ell(\lambda)\leq k+1
, then
we have

(4.7)

\alpha(\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=g_{\lambda}.

In particular, we have

(4.8)

\alpha(\mathcal{O}_{R_{i}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=\tau_{i}.

Proof.

We know from Proposition

2.9
that
\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda}=\tilde{g}_{\lambda}.

Therefore, using Proposition
2.5
, we see that

\alpha(\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=\sigma^{-1}(\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda})=\sigma^{-1}(\tilde{g}_{\lambda})=g_{\lambda}.

∎

4.4.
Correspondence of Schubert bases

We consider the extended affine symmetric group
\hat{S}_{k+1}
,
which is generated by
\{s_{i}\;|\;i\in I\}\cup\{\pi\}
satisfying
the same relations among
s_{i}
’s and

\pi^{k+1}=id,\quad\pi s_{i}=s_{i+1}\pi.

We have
\hat{S}_{k+1}\cong S_{k+1}\ltimes P^{\vee}
, where

P^{\vee}
is the coweight lattice of
\mathrm{SL}_{k+1}(\mathbb{C})
.
The translation element associated to
-\varpi_{i}^{\vee}\in P^{\vee}
is explicitly given by

t_{-\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-i}x_{R_{i}}.

Example 4.7
.

For
k=3
,

(4.9)

\displaystyle t_{-\varpi_{1}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{0},\quad t_{-\varpi_{2}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-2}s_{0}s_{3}s_{1}s_{0},\quad t_{-\varpi_{3}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-3}s_{2}s_{1}s_{0}.

Let
w\in S_{k+1}
be an
i
-
Grassmannian permutation
, i.e.,
\mathrm{Des}(w)=\{i\}.
The set of all
i
-Grassmannian permutations in
S_{k+1}
is in bijection with
\mathcal{P}_{i}^{k+1-i}.

Explicitly, for an
i
-Grassmannian permutation
w
in
S_{k+1}
,
the corresponding partition
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{i}^{k+1-i}
is given by

(4.10)

\lambda_{i+1-j}=w(j)-j\quad(1\leq j\leq i).

For each partition
\lambda
in
\mathcal{P}_{i}^{k+1-i}
, we denote the corresponding

i
-Grassmannian permutation by
w_{\lambda,i}.

For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k+1-i}_{i}
,
the
dual
partition of
\lambda
is the element

\lambda^{\vee}

in
\mathcal{P}^{k+1-i}_{i}
defined by
\lambda^{\vee}_{j}=k+1-i-\lambda_{i+1-j}\;(1\leq j\leq i).

Proposition 4.8

(
[
13
]
)
.

Let
w_{\lambda,i}\in S_{k+1}
be an
i
-Grassmannian permutation.
Then

(4.11)

\Phi_{k+1}({\mathfrak{G}_{\lambda,i}})=\frac{g_{(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}}}{\tau_{i}},

where
(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}
is the conjugate of
\lambda^{\vee}
.

Proof.

Let
\Phi_{k+1}^{\prime}
be the map in
[
13
]
.
Recall that for
w\in S_{k+1}
,
\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{w}
is identified with
\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q}\;\mathrm{mod}\;I_{k+1}
.

[
13
, Theorem 7.1]
reads

\Phi_{k+1}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{G}_{w_{\lambda,i}}^{Q}\;\mathrm{mod}\;I_{k+1})={g_{\lambda^{\vee}}}/{g_{(k+1-i)^{i}}}.

From Remark
4.4
, we deduce (
4.11
).
∎

In order to describe
the image
\Phi_{k+1}(\mathcal{O}^{w}_{G/B})
,
we need a map
S_{k+1}\rightarrow\mathcal{P}^{k},\;w\mapsto\theta_{k}(w)
, due to Lam and Shimozono
[
24
, Lemma 11]
.

Proposition 4.9

(
[
24
]
)
.

Let
w\in S_{k+1}
. There is a
k
-bounded partition
\theta_{k}(w)
such that

(4.12)

wt_{-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}i}\cdot x_{\theta_{k}(w)}.

Proof.

One can show that the left-hand side of (
4.12
) is an affine Grassmannian element in
\hat{S}_{k+1}=\langle\pi\rangle\ltimes\tilde{S}_{k+1}
(see the first part of the proof of Lemma 6.1 in
[
24
]
). Then
such an element can be uniquely written in the form on the right-hand side of (
4.12
) for a
k
-bounded partition, which we denote by
\theta_{k}(w)
.
∎

For an
i
-Grassmannian permutation
w=w_{\lambda,i}
,
we have

\theta_{k}(w)=(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}
(
[
13
, Lemma 7.1]
).
See §
B
, for another direct proof of this fact.

The next result is a refined version of
[
13
, Conjecture 1.8]
.

Theorem 4.10
.

For
w\in S_{k+1}
, we have

(4.13)

\Phi_{k+1}(\mathfrak{G}_{w})=\frac{\sigma^{-1}(\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\theta_{k}(w)})}{\prod_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}\tau_{i}}.

Proof.

Let
Q^{\vee}
denote the coroot lattice of
\mathrm{SL}_{k+1}(\mathbb{C}).

Then we have
\tilde{S}_{k+1}\cong S_{k+1}\ltimes Q^{\vee}
.
We denote by
t_{\beta}\in\tilde{S}_{k+1}
be translation element corresponding to
\beta\in Q^{\vee}.

Let
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})_{\mathrm{loc}}
be the localization of
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})
by
the multiplicative set generated by
\mathcal{O}_{t_{\beta}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\;(\beta\in{Q}^{\vee}).

Kato
[
15
, Corollary 4.15]
constructed an injective ring homomorphism

\kappa:K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})_{\mathrm{loc}}\hookrightarrow{QK}(G/B)_{\mathrm{loc}}

such that

(4.14)

\kappa\left(\mathcal{O}_{{wt_{\beta}}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\cdot(\mathcal{O}_{t_{\gamma}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1}\right)=Q^{\beta-\gamma}\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{w}\quad(w\in S_{k+1}),

where
\beta,\gamma\in-Q^{\vee}
such that
wt_{\beta}\in\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0}
and
\gamma
is strictly antidominant, and
Q^{\beta-\gamma}
is defined by identifying

Q^{\alpha_{i}^{\vee}}
with
Q_{i}.

Since
\mathcal{O}_{R_{i}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}
corresponds to
\tau_{i}=g_{R_{i}}
by
\alpha
(Proposition
4.6
),
the isomorphism
\alpha
yields

K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})_{\mathrm{loc}}\cong\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1}\;(1\leq i\leq k)].

Let
\kappa^{\prime}
be the composition

\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}:K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})_{\mathrm{loc}}

\displaystyle\cong\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1}]\quad\text{(induced by $\alpha$)}

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1},(\tau_{i}^{+})^{-1}]

\displaystyle\underset{\Phi_{k+1}^{-1}}{\cong}A_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}[Q_{i}^{-1}]\quad\text{(Theorem \ref{thm:IIM})}

\displaystyle\underset{\phi}{\hookrightarrow}QK(G/B)[Q_{i}^{-1}]\quad\text{ (Corollary \ref{cor:phi})}.

We claim that
\kappa^{\prime}=\kappa.

Note that
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})
is generated by
\mathcal{O}_{s_{i-1}\cdots s_{1}s_{0}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}=\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\;(1\leq i\leq k),

and that
\alpha(\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=g_{(i)}.

For
1\leq i\leq k
, let
u_{i}\in S_{k+1}
be the
k
-Grassmannian permutation of shape
(1^{k-i})
.
So by Proposition
4.8
, we have

\Phi_{k+1}(\mathfrak{G}_{u_{i}}^{Q})=\frac{g_{(i)}}{\tau_{k}}.

Hence it follows that

\kappa^{\prime}(\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\cdot(\mathcal{O}_{R_{k}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1})=\phi(\mathfrak{G}^{Q}_{u_{i}})=\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{u_{i}}.

By Lemma
B.3
, we have

\theta_{k}(u_{i})=(i)
.
Therefore, we have
\mathcal{O}_{u_{i}t_{-\varpi_{k}^{\vee}}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}=\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}
, and hence by the definition of
\kappa

\kappa(\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\cdot(\mathcal{O}_{R_{k}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1})=\mathcal{O}^{u_{i}}_{G/B}.

Since
(\mathcal{O}_{R_{k}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1}
is an invertible element,
we have
\kappa^{\prime}(\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}})=\kappa(\mathcal{O}_{(i)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}),

and hence
\kappa^{\prime}=\kappa.

For
w\in S_{k+1}
,
we deduce that
\mathcal{O}_{wt_{-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}}^{\mathrm{Gr}}=\mathcal{O}_{\theta_{k}(w)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}
by Proposition
4.9
,
and hence see that

\displaystyle\phi(\mathfrak{G}_{w}^{Q})=\mathcal{O}^{w}_{G/B}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\kappa\left(\mathcal{O}_{\theta_{k}(w)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\cdot\prod_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}(\mathcal{O}_{R_{i}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}\left(\mathcal{O}_{\theta_{k}(w)}^{\mathrm{Gr}}\cdot\prod_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}(\mathcal{O}_{R_{i}}^{\mathrm{Gr}})^{-1}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\phi\circ\Phi_{k+1}^{-1})\left(\sigma^{-1}(\tilde{g}_{\theta_{k}(w)})\cdot\prod_{i\in\mathrm{Des}(w)}\tau_{i}^{-1}\right)\quad(\text{by \eqref{eq:alphaO}}).

Since
\phi
is injective we obtain (
4.13
).
∎

4.5.
Localizations of
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})

The isomorphism conjectured by Lam, Li, Mihalcea, and Shimozono in
[
20
]
is
different from
\Phi_{k+1}
in the way of
localization of
K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr}).
The localization of

K_{*}(\mathrm{Gr})
in
[
20
]
can be identified with

\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1}\;(1\leq i\leq k)],

while our version is

\Lambda_{(k)}[\tau_{i}^{-1},\;(\tau_{i}^{+})^{-1}\;(1\leq i\leq k)].

The aim of this section is to clarify the geometric meaning of
\tau_{i}^{+}=\tilde{g}_{R_{i}}\in\Lambda_{(k)}
.

Lemma 4.11
.

\tau_{i}^{2}-\tau_{i-1}\tau_{i+1}=\tau_{i}^{+}\cdot\tau_{i}^{-}.

Proof.

This is the discrete Toda equation given by Hirota
[
12
]
.
We can show this by comparing the construction of
\Phi_{k+1}

[
13
]
and the Lax formalism for the discrete Toda equation given in
[
14
, Section 1]
.
∎

Lemma 4.12
.

For
1\leq i\leq k
,

\Phi_{k+1}(1-Q_{i})=\dfrac{\tau_{i}^{+}\cdot\tau_{i}^{-}}{\tau_{i}^{2}}.

Proof.

This follows from Lemma
4.11
.
∎

Lemma 4.13
.

For
1\leq i\leq k+1
,

\tau_{i}=g_{R_{i}^{*}}+\tau_{i}^{-}.

Proof.

It suffices to show that
\sigma(\tau_{i}-g_{R_{i}^{*}})=\tau_{i}.

This follows from (
2.3
), because
R_{i}^{*}
is the unique maximal proper
element among the partitions

\mu\subset R_{i}.

∎

Proposition 4.14
.

For
1\leq i\leq k
,

({1-Q_{i}})z_{1}\cdots z_{i}=1-\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{s_{i}}

in
QK(G/B).

Proof.

By
\Phi_{k+1}(\mathcal{O}^{s_{i}})=g_{R_{i}^{*}}/\tau_{i}
(
[
13
, Theorem 1.7]
),
and Lemma
4.13
,
the image of the right hand side is

1-\frac{g_{R_{i}^{*}}}{\tau_{i}}=\frac{\tau_{i}-g_{R_{i}^{*}}}{\tau_{i}}=\frac{\tau_{i}^{-}}{\tau_{i}}.

On the other hand,

\Phi_{k+1}((1-Q_{i})z_{1}\cdots z_{i})=\frac{\tau_{i}^{-}\tau_{i}^{+}}{\tau_{i}^{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{i}\frac{\tau_{j}\tau_{j-1}^{+}}{\tau_{j}^{+}\tau_{j-1}}=\frac{\tau_{i}^{-}}{\tau_{i}}.

∎

Remark 4.15
.

The result above corresponds to
Corollary 3.33 in
[
27
]
;
note also that

1-\mathcal{O}_{G/B}^{s_{i}}=\mathcal{O}_{G/B}(-\varpi_{i}).

Corollary 4.16
.

The following element

Q_{t_{\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}}^{-1}(1-Q_{i})^{-1}(1-\mathcal{O}^{s_{i}}_{G/B})

in
QK(G/B)_{\mathrm{loc}}
is
sent to
1/\tau^{+}_{i}

by
\Phi_{k+1},

where
Q_{t_{\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}}
is the element such that
\Phi_{k+1}(Q_{t_{\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}})=\tau_{i}.

Note that the factor

Q_{t_{\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}}
is invertible
in
QK(G/B)_{\mathrm{loc}}
. Hence up to an invertible factor,

1/\tau_{i}^{+}

corresponds to the
element
(1-Q_{i})^{-1}(1-\mathcal{O}^{s_{i}}_{G/B})

of
QK(G/B)\subset QK(G/B)_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Appendix A
Parabolic quotient of Coxeter groups

We discuss some properties of a coset space of a Coxeter group.
Our basic reference is Bjorner-Brenti
[
4
]
.
Let
(W,S)
be a
Coxeter system
(see
[
4
]
for the definition), where
W
is the group generated by
S=\{s_{i}\;|\;i\in I\}

with index set
I
.
The
Bruhat order
on
W
(see
[
4
, Chapter 2]
) is
denoted by
\leq.

Let
J
be any subset of
I
.
Let
W_{J}
be the subgroup of
W
generated by
s_{i}\;(i\in J).

The
minimal coset representatives

W^{J}
of the quotient
W/W_{J}

is defined to be
W^{J}:=\{w\in W\;|\;ws_{i}>w\;\mbox{for all}\;i\in J\}
.
Any element
w
of
W
is expressed uniquely as
w=w^{J}w_{J}
, with
w_{J}\in W_{J}
and
w^{J}\in W^{J}
(
[
4
, Proposition 2.4.4]
).

The following result
is well-known and used throughout this section.

Lemma A.1
.

Let
x\in W^{J}
and
i\in I
. Then,

s_{i}x<x\Longrightarrow s_{i}x\in W^{J}
.

A.1.
Proof of Proposition
3.13

The
0
-
Hecke algebra

H_{W}
is the associative
\mathbb{C}
-algebra generated by

\{T_{i}\;|\;i\in I\}
subject to the same relations as those for
W
except
T_{i}^{2}=-T_{i}
in place of
s_{i}^{2}=id
. For
w\in W
, define
T_{w}=T_{i_{1}}\cdots T_{i_{m}}
for any reduced expression
w=s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{m}}.

The elements
T_{w}\;(w\in W)
form a basis of
H_{W}.

Proposition A.2
.

Let
V^{J}
be a left
H_{W}
module given by

V^{J}=H_{W}e_{J},\quad e_{J}:=\sum_{w\in W_{J}}T_{w}.

Then,
V^{J}=\bigoplus_{x\in W^{J}}\mathbb{C}a_{x}

with

a_{x}:=T_{x}e_{J}
, and for
i\in I
,

(A.1)

T_{i}\cdot a_{x}=\begin{cases}a_{s_{i}x}&(s_{i}x>x\;\mbox{and}\;s_{i}x\in W^{J})\\
-a_{x}&(s_{i}x<x)\\
0&(s_{i}x>x\;\mbox{and}\;s_{i}x\notin W^{J})\end{cases}.

Proof.

For
i\in J
, we will prove
T_{i}e_{J}=0.

Let

X^{+}=\{v\in W\;|\;s_{i}v>v\}
and
X^{-}=\{v\in W\;|\;s_{i}v<v\}
.
We have
s_{i}(X^{\pm})=X^{\mp}.

If
v\in X^{+}
, then
T_{i}T_{v}=T_{s_{i}v}
.
If
v\in X^{-}
, then
T_{v}=T_{i}T_{s_{i}v}
, and hence

T_{i}T_{v}=T_{i}^{2}T_{s_{i}v}=-T_{i}T_{s_{i}v}=-T_{v}.

Therefore,

T_{i}e_{J}=\sum_{v\in X^{+}}T_{i}T_{v}+\sum_{v\in X^{-}}T_{i}T_{v}=\sum_{v\in X^{+}}T_{s_{i}v}-\sum_{v\in X^{-}}T_{v}=0.

If
v\notin W^{J}
, then it is easy to see that there is
a reduced expression
v=s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{m}}
with
i_{m}\in J
.
Hence
T_{v}e_{J}=T_{s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{m-1}}}T_{i_{m}}e_{J}=0
.
It follows that
\{a_{x}\}_{x\in W^{J}}

spans
V^{J}=H_{W}e_{J}
. Note that for
x\in W^{J}
and
v\in W_{J}
, we have

T_{x}T_{v}=T_{xv}
since
\ell(xv)=\ell(x)+\ell(v)
(
[
4
, Proposition 2.4.4 (2)]
); the linear independence of
\{a_{x}\}_{x\in W^{J}}
follows from this fact.

Let
x\in W^{J}
.
If
s_{i}x>x
, then

T_{i}\cdot a_{x}=T_{i}\cdot T_{x}e_{J}=T_{s_{i}x}e_{J}=\begin{cases}a_{s_{i}x}&(s_{i}x\in W^{J})\\
0&(s_{i}x\notin W^{J})\end{cases}.

If
s_{i}x<x
, then
T_{i}\cdot a_{x}=T_{i}T_{x}e_{J}=-T_{x}e_{J}=-a_{x}.

∎

Proposition A.3
.

For
x\in W^{J}
, let
b_{x}:=\sum_{y\leq x}a_{y}.

Set
D_{i}=T_{i}+1\;(i\in I)
.
Then

(A.2)

D_{i}\cdot b_{x}=\begin{cases}b_{s_{i}x}&(s_{i}x\in W^{J},\;s_{i}x>x)\\
b_{x}&(\mbox{otherwise})\end{cases}.

Lemma A.4

(
Z
-lemma)
.

Let
w,v\in W
and
i\in I
.
Suppse
s_{i}w>w
and
s_{i}v>v
.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:

(1)\;w\leq v,\quad(2)\;s_{i}w\leq s_{i}v,\quad(3)\;w\leq s_{i}v.

Proof.

[
30
, Proposition 5.4.3]
.
∎

Lemma A.5
.

Let
x\in W^{J}
and
i\in I.
We set

\displaystyle X_{\leq x}^{+}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\{y\in W^{J}\;|\;y\leq x,\;s_{i}y\in W^{J},\;s_{i}y>y\},

\displaystyle X_{\leq x}^{-}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\{y\in W^{J}\;|\;y\leq x,\;s_{i}y\in W^{J},\;s_{i}y<y\},

\displaystyle X^{0}_{\leq x}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\{y\in W^{J}\;|\;y\leq x,\;s_{i}y\notin W^{J}\}.

(1)

If
s_{i}x\in W^{J},\;s_{i}x>x
, then

s_{i}(X^{+}_{\leq x})=X^{-}_{\leq s_{i}x},\;X^{+}_{\leq x}=X_{\leq s_{i}x}^{+},\;X^{0}_{\leq x}=X_{\leq s_{i}x}^{0}.

(2)

If
s_{i}x\in W^{J},\;s_{i}x<x
, then
s_{i}(X_{\leq x}^{+})=X_{\leq x}^{-}.

(3)

If
s_{i}x\notin W^{J}
, then
s_{i}(X_{\leq x}^{+})=X_{\leq x}^{-}.

Proof.

(1) and (2) follow immediately from Lemma
A.4
.
(3) The inclusion
s_{i}(X_{\leq x}^{+})\supset X_{\leq x}^{-}
follows from Lemma
A.4
.
We will show that
s_{i}(X_{\leq x}^{+})\subset X_{\leq x}^{-}.

Take arbitrary
z\in s_{i}(X_{\leq x}^{+})
. Write
z=s_{i}y
with
y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}.
Since
s_{i}z=s_{i}^{2}y=y<s_{i}y=z
,
it suffices to prove
s_{i}y\leq x.

Since
x\in W^{J}
and
s_{i}x\notin W^{J}
, we have
s_{i}x>x

by Lemma
A.1
. Hence it follows from
Lemma
A.4
that
s_{i}x\geq s_{i}y
. Also, it follows from

[
4
, Corollary 2.5.2]
that
there is
v\in W_{J}
such that
s_{i}x=xv
; in fact, we can take
v=s_{j}
for some
j\in J.

Hence we have
xv\geq s_{i}y
.
Here note that
s_{i}y\in W^{J}
as
y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}
.
It follows that

s_{i}y=(s_{i}y)^{J}\leq(xv)^{J}=x^{J}=x;

here we used the fact that
w\leq v
for
w,v\in W
implies

w^{J}\leq v^{J}

(
[
4
, Proposition 2.5.1]
).
∎

Proof of Proposition
A.3
.

We have
b_{x}=\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{-}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{0}}a_{y}
.
Using (
A.1
), it is straightforward to verify

\displaystyle D_{i}\cdot b_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}}a_{s_{i}y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{0}}a_{y}.

Consider first the case that
s_{i}x\in W^{J},\;s_{i}x>x.

From Lemma
A.5
(1), we see that

\displaystyle D_{i}\cdot b_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{y\in X_{\leq s_{i}x}^{-}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq s_{i}x}^{+}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq s_{i}x}^{0}}a_{y}=b_{s_{i}x}.

Next consider the case that
s_{i}x\in W^{J},s_{i}x<x
. We see that

s_{i}(X^{+}_{\leq x})=X_{\leq x}^{-}
by Lemma
A.5
(2), and hence we see that

D_{i}\cdot b_{x}=\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{-}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{+}}a_{y}+\sum_{y\in X_{\leq x}^{0}}a_{y}=b_{x}.

Finally we consider the case that
s_{i}x\notin W^{J}
. We have

s_{i}(X^{+}_{\leq x})=X_{\leq x}^{-}
by Lemma
A.5
(3),
and hence
D_{i}\cdot b_{x}=b_{x}
by exactly the same reasoning as in the previous case.
∎

Proof of Proposition
3.13
.

We apply Proposition
A.2
to

W=\tilde{S}_{k+1}=\langle s_{i}\;|\;i=0,1,\ldots,k\rangle
,

W_{J}=S_{k+1},\;W^{J}=\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0}
with
J=\{1,2,\ldots,k\}
,
and define an isomorphism

V^{J}\rightarrow\Lambda_{(k)}
of vector spaces by

a_{x}\mapsto\overset{\circ}{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda},b_{x}\mapsto\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}^{(k)}_{\lambda}

under the bijection
W^{J}=\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0}\ni x\mapsto\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}
.
Then we obtain Proposition
3.13
.
∎

A.2.
Proof of Lemma
3.18

For
w\in W
, and
i\in I
, we define
s_{i}*w

in the same way as in (
2.4
).
Let
\mathcal{S}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{r})
be a
sequence
of elements of
I
, and
w\in S
. We define

(A.3)

\mathcal{S}*w=s_{i_{1}}*(s_{i_{2}}*\cdots*(s_{i_{r}}*w)\cdots).

Proposition A.6
.

Let
\mathcal{S}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{r})
be a
sequence of elements of
I.

Set
|\mathcal{S}|=r
, and
T_{\mathcal{S}}:=T_{i_{1}}\cdots T_{i_{r}}\in H_{W}.
Then for
x\in W^{J}
, we have

T_{\mathcal{S}}\cdot a_{x}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{|\mathcal{S}|-\ell(\mathcal{S}*x)+\ell(x)}a_{\mathcal{S}*x}&(\mathcal{S}*x\in W^{J})\\
0&(\mathcal{S}*x\notin W^{J})\end{cases}.

Proof.

For
1\leq p\leq r
, set
\mathcal{S}_{p}=(i_{p},\ldots,i_{r})
, and
\mathcal{S}_{r+1}=\varnothing.

We use decreasing induction on
p
.
If
p=r+1
, then the assertion is obvious. Suppose
1\leq p<r+1
.
We first consider the case that
\mathcal{S}_{p}*x\notin W^{J}.

Let
q\;(\geq p)
be the maximal integer such that
\mathcal{S}_{q}*x\notin W^{J}.

Then, we have
\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x\in W^{J}
,
\mathcal{S}_{q}*x=s_{i_{q}}*(\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x)=s_{i_{q}}(\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x)\notin W^{J}
, and so

s_{i_{q}}(\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x)>\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x
by Lemma
A.1
.
Therefore,
T_{i_{q}}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x}=0.

By the inductive hypothesis,
we deduce that
T_{i_{q+1}}\cdots T_{i_{r}}\cdot a_{x}=\pm a_{\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x}
, and hence

T_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\cdot a_{x}=T_{i_{p}}\cdots T_{i_{q}}(T_{i_{q+1}}\cdots T_{i_{r}}\cdot a_{x})=\pm T_{i_{p}}\cdots T_{i_{q}}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{q+1}*x}=0.

Next we consider the case when
\mathcal{S}_{p}*x\in W^{J}.

Note that, in view of Lemma
A.1
,
we have
\mathcal{S}_{q}*x\in W^{J}
for
p\leq q\leq r+1
.
By the inductive hypothesis, we have

T_{i_{p+1}}\cdots T_{i_{r}}a_{x}=(-1)^{r-p-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)+\ell(x)}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}
, so

(A.4)

T_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\cdot a_{x}=T_{i_{p}}\cdot(T_{i_{p+1}}\cdots T_{i_{r}}a_{x})=(-1)^{r-p-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)+\ell(x)}T_{i_{p}}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}.

Now we consider two cases : (a)
s_{i_{p}}(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)>\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x
, (b)
s_{i_{p}}(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)<\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x.

If (a) holds, then
s_{i_{p}}(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)=s_{i_{p}}*(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)=\mathcal{S}_{p}*x\in W^{J}.
Therefore,

T_{i_{p}}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}=a_{s_{i_{p}}(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)}=a_{\mathcal{S}_{p}*x},

and hence by (
A.4
),

T_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\cdot a_{x}=(-1)^{r-p-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)+\ell(x)}T_{i_{p}}a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}=(-1)^{r-p-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)+\ell(x)}a_{\mathcal{S}_{p}*x};

the sign is correct
since we have
\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)=\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p}*x)-1.

Suppose (b) holds.
Note that
\mathcal{S}_{p}*x=\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x\in W^{J}
by (
A.3
). By the definition of
T_{i_{p}}
,

T_{i_{p}}\cdot a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}=-a_{\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x}=-a_{\mathcal{S}_{p}*x}.

Hence we deduce that

T_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\cdot a_{x}=(-1)^{r-p-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x)+\ell(x)}(-a_{\mathcal{S}_{p}*x})=(-1)^{r-p+1-\ell(\mathcal{S}_{p}*x)+\ell(x)}a_{\mathcal{S}_{p}*x},

where we again used
\mathcal{S}_{p}*x=\mathcal{S}_{p+1}*x.

This completes the proof.
∎

Proof of Lemma
3.18
.

Let
A\subsetneq I
, with
|A|=r
, and take a reduced expression

s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{r}}
for
u_{A}
.
We apply Proposition
A.6
to the sequence
\mathcal{S}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{r})
.
Then
T_{\mathcal{S}}=T_{u_{A}}
and we obtain Lemma
3.18
.
∎

Appendix B
Grassmannian permutations

An explicit description of
\theta_{k}(w)
is available (see
[
24
, §6]
).
For the reader’s convenience, we include a simple direct proof
when
w
is a Grassmannian element
w_{\lambda,i}
(Lemma
B.3
).

Proposition B.1
.

Let
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}
be a
k
-bounded partition of size
r
such that
\lambda_{1}+\ell(\lambda)\leq k+1
.
Take any standard tableau
T
of shape
\lambda
.
We denote the box of
\lambda
with entry
i
in
T
by
b_{T}(i).

Then
s_{\mathrm{res}(b_{T}(r))}\cdots s_{\mathrm{res}(b_{T}(2))}s_{\mathrm{res}(b_{T}(1))}
is a reduced
expression for
x_{\lambda}
.

Proof.

We note first that the corresponding fact
is well-known for the
i
-Grassmannian permutation
w_{\lambda,i}
.
The reader can consult
[
6
, §3.1]

for an exposition of this fact in a more general setting.

Since
\lambda_{1}+\ell(\lambda)\leq k+1
, there is

1\leq i\leq k
such that

\lambda\subset R_{k+1-i}
. Then in the reduced
expression of
x_{\lambda}
given by (
2.1
),
s_{k+1-i}
does not appear.
Hence
x_{\lambda}\in\langle s_{-i+1},\ldots,s_{-i+k}\rangle\cong S_{k+1};

the isomorphism of groups
\phi:S_{k+1}\rightarrow\langle s_{-i+1},\ldots,s_{-i+k}\rangle
is given by
\phi(s_{j})=s_{-i+j}
.
Then, the result follows from the case for the
i
-Grassmannian permutation.
∎

Remark B.2
.

An element in a Coxeter group
W
is
fully commutative
if
any two of its reduced expressions are related by a series of transpositions of adjacent commuting generators.
It is well-known that any
i
-Grassmannian element in
S_{k+1}
is
fully commutative.
From the above proof, we see that if
\lambda_{1}+\ell(\lambda)\leq k+1
, then

x_{\lambda}
is fully commutative.

Lemma B.3
.

Let
\lambda
be a partition contained in
R_{k+1-i}=(k+1-i)^{i}
, and
w_{\lambda,i}\in S_{k+1}
the corresponding

i
-Grassmannian permutation. Then
\theta_{k}(w_{\lambda,i})=(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}.

Proof.

In the extended affine symmetric group

\hat{S}_{k+1}
, we compute

w_{\lambda,i}t_{-\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}=w_{\lambda,i}\pi^{-i}x_{R_{i}}=\pi^{-i}(\pi^{i}w_{\lambda,i}\pi^{-i})x_{R_{i}}.

A reduced expression for
y_{\lambda}:=\pi^{i}w_{\lambda,i}\pi^{-i}
is
obtained by replacing
s_{j}
with
s_{j+i}
in
w_{\lambda,i}
. It is straightforward to see
when we reflect the tableau of
y_{\lambda}
along the line with a slope of
1
,
it fits inside the tableau of shape
R_{i}
filled with
(k+1)
-residues adjusted to the south-east corner (see Example
B.4
below).
Let
T
be the standard tableau with shape
R_{i}

that is obtained by filling positive integers into each row of
(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}
from
left to right, with rows taken from top to bottom, and then into each column
of the remaining boxes from top to bottom, with columns taken from left to right.
Then apply Proposition
B.1

to
T
.
The obtained reduced expression for

x_{R_{i}}
shows
x_{R_{i}}=y_{\lambda}^{-1}\cdot x_{(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}},

and hence
w_{\lambda,i}t_{-\varpi_{i}^{\vee}}=\pi^{-i}x_{(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}}
, showing

\theta_{k}(w_{\lambda,i})=(\lambda^{\vee})^{\prime}.

∎

Example B.4
.

For

Appendix C
Vertical Pieri rule for the closed
K
-
k
-Schur functions

A Pieri rule for
\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda}
was proved by Takigiku
[
40
]
.
We record here the vertical version of Takigiku’s formula,
which should be known to experts but is missing in the literature.
We do not use this result in the main part of this paper.

For
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}
,

1\leq r\leq r,
define

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\{A\subsetneq I\;\left|\;|A|=r,\;d_{A}x_{\lambda}\in\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0},\;d_{A}x_{\lambda}\geq_{L}x_{\lambda}\}\right.,

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\{A\subsetneq I\;\left|\;|A|=r,\;u_{A}x_{\lambda}\in\tilde{S}_{k+1}^{0},\;u_{A}x_{\lambda}\geq_{L}x_{\lambda}\}\right..

For an element
A
in

\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}
, we write
d_{A}x_{\lambda}=x_{\kappa}
for
an element
\kappa\in\mathcal{P}^{k},
and denote this
\kappa
by
d_{A}\lambda
.
Similarly, for an element
A
in

\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}
, we write
u_{A}x_{\lambda}=x_{\kappa}
for
an element
\kappa\in\mathcal{P}^{k},
and denote this
\kappa
by
u_{A}\lambda
.

Example C.1
.

For
k=3
,
\lambda=(2,1)\in\mathcal{P}^{3},

and
r=2
, we have (see Figure
2
)

\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}=\{\{2,3\},\{0,2\}\},\quad d_{\{2,3\}}=s_{3}s_{2},\quad d_{\{0,2\}}=s_{0}s_{2}=s_{2}s_{0},

\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}=\{\{1,2\},\{0,2\}\},\quad u_{\{1,2\}}=s_{1}s_{2},\quad u_{\{0,2\}}=s_{0}s_{2}=s_{2}s_{0}.

The corresponding weak (horizontal and vertical) strips are given by

d_{\{2,3\}}\lambda=(3,1,1),\quad d_{\{0,2\}}\lambda=u_{\{0,2\}}\lambda=(2,1,1),\quad u_{\{1,2\}}\lambda=(2,1,1,1).

For
A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}
, it is known by Takigiku
[
40
, Corollary 4.8]
that

A_{1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r^{\prime}}^{(k)}
, with

r^{\prime}=|A_{1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{m}|
and hence

d_{A_{1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{m}}\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}

is defined.

Proposition C.2
.

Let
A\mapsto\overline{A}
be
the map given by sending
i\in A
to
-i\in\overline{A}.

Then for
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}
, and
1\leq r\leq k,

\overline{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}}=\mathcal{V}_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}},r}^{(k)}.

Proof.

Let
A\in\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}
.
Recall that
\omega_{k}

is an automorphism of the group
\tilde{S}_{k+1}
preserving the left weak order. Therefore, it follows that

u_{\overline{A}}x_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}}}=\omega_{k}(d_{A})\omega_{k}(x_{\lambda})=\omega_{k}({d_{A}x_{\lambda}})\geq_{L}\omega_{k}(x_{\lambda})=x_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}}},

and hence
\overline{A}\in\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}.

Thus
\overline{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}}\subset\mathcal{V}_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}},r}^{(k)}
.
Similarly we have
\overline{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}}\supset\mathcal{V}_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}},r}^{(k)}
.
∎

Theorem C.3

(
[
39
]
)
.

Let
\lambda\in\mathcal{P}^{k}
and
1\leq r\leq k
.
Let

\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}=\{A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\},\quad\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,r}^{(k)}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{n}\}.

Then

\displaystyle\tilde{g}_{(r)}\cdot\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{1\leq a_{1}<\cdots<a_{i}\leq m}\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{d_{A_{a_{1}}\cap\cdots\cap A_{a_{i}}}\lambda},

\displaystyle\tilde{g}_{(1^{r})}\cdot\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{1\leq a_{1}<\cdots<a_{i}\leq n}\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{u_{B_{a_{1}}\cap\cdots\cap B_{a_{i}}}\lambda}.

Proof.

(
C.3
) is due to Takigiku
[
39
]
.
From Proposition
C.2
, it follows that

\{\overline{A_{1}},\ldots,\overline{A_{m}}\}=\mathcal{V}_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}},r}^{(k)}.

By applying
\Omega
to both sides of the equation, we obtain

\tilde{g}_{(1^{r})}\cdot\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{\lambda^{\omega_{k}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{1\leq a_{1}<\cdots<a_{i}\leq m}\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{u_{\overline{A_{a_{1}}}\cap\cdots\cap\overline{A_{a_{i}}}}\lambda^{\omega_{k}}},

where we used

\Omega(\tilde{g}_{(r)})=\tilde{g}_{(1^{r})}
and

\Omega(\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{d_{A_{a_{1}}\cap\cdots\cap A_{a_{i}}}\lambda})=\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{u_{\overline{A_{a_{1}}\cap\cdots\cap A_{a_{i}}}}\lambda^{\omega_{k}}}=\tilde{g}^{(k)}_{u_{\overline{A_{a_{1}}}\cap\cdots\cap\overline{A_{a_{i}}}}\lambda^{\omega_{k}}}.

Thus we have (
C.3
).
∎
